rationale: Start with a broad gradient to observe all 10 compounds and locate the elution window while limiting the time penalty. The retention pattern and weakest resolutions will guide window trimming and subsequent slope and temperature tests.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the two critical early pairs respond to slope. This diagnostic run will distinguish slope-sensitive overlap from selectivity that may require a temperature change.

Test temperature selectivity against injection 1 while keeping the gradient unchanged. Higher temperature should shorten late retention and may separate the early cluster without requiring a longer gradient.

At 60 C only one pair remains below target, and there is nearly two minutes of retention-time headroom. A shallower gradient will test whether that pair can reach full resolution while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair became less resolved with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient instead. This also shortens the run while checking whether the neighboring early pair retains adequate resolution.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at a slope close to injection 3 to shift selectivity within the early cluster. The first peak has retention headroom, and changing the gradient window may improve the pair that responded poorly to slope alone.
Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark and shorten the gradient by one grid step. This tests whether full resolution can be preserved with an earlier last peak.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness relative to injection 7 to recover the small resolution deficits while retaining an eight-minute gradient. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.
Lower the endpoint one more grid step to bring the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. This should preserve a last-peak time shorter than injection 6 while recovering the maximum CRF.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction can preserve full resolution while shortening retention further. Injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; this run probes the early-cluster selectivity and first-pair compression at phi0 = 0.20.

Test a modest temperature reduction at the nearly resolved, faster method from injection 7. Temperature may rebalance the two marginal early pairs and recover full resolution without lengthening the gradient.

Return to 60 C and test whether a shallower gradient rescues the single critical pair at phi0 = 0.20. This explores an alternative fully resolved window, while retaining injection 9 as the fastest maximum-score method.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test the opposite temperature extreme for a different elution order that could permit a faster fully resolved method. The steep, high-endpoint gradient limits late retention while probing this alternative selectivity regime.

Return to the successful high-temperature window and make the gradient slightly shallower to build resolution margin above injection 9's marginal R = 1.51. This should retain the maximum CRF with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten injection 12's gradient to lift its sole marginal pair from R = 1.47 toward full resolution. This tests whether the higher-starting-organic window provides another maximum-score method with useful selectivity margin.

Trim the endpoint and gradient duration together, keeping the slope slightly shallower than the fully resolved injection 9. The last peak is expected near the gradient end, testing a shorter programmed gradient without sacrificing the maximum CRF.

With maximum CRF secured, test a shallower gradient in the successful trimmed window to increase the critical-pair resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, so the added separation need not incur a time penalty.

Test a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary more closely. This should place the last peak near 5.9 minutes, though the critical pair may sit just below R = 1.5.

Injection 18 still has a subthreshold pair despite its rounded CRF, so injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test the intermediate starting fraction to check whether it offers a better balance between the two critical early separations.

Return to the best starting fraction and test the endpoint between injections 9 and 14. This should preserve maximum CRF with a little more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method and less retention time than injection 14.

Preserve injection 9's successful gradient slope while shortening the programmed ramp to four minutes. The final peaks will elute during the hold, so this tests whether a lower-organic, shorter-ramp method can retain full resolution and finish eluting within 10 minutes.

Preserve injection 14's fully resolving slope while trimming the gradient to end near the last peak's elution composition. This should retain its resolution margin with little hold-related delay, unlike the lower endpoint in injection 21.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 14 and 17 to obtain additional resolution margin while keeping all peaks inside the gradient and below 10 minutes. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run evaluates a less marginal alternative.

Test one endpoint step below injection 17 to increase critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Use the final injection to test one more step toward greater critical-pair resolution margin, with the last peak expected around 9 minutes and no time penalty. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the campaign has already reached the maximum CRF.
